text: Every email notification you'll ever build in ServiceNow is a row on one single table: sysevent_email_action. Open System Notification, then Email, then Notifications in the navigator, and you're looking at a list view of that exact table. A notification record bundles together three things — what has to happen for it to fire, who should receive it, and what the email actually says — and this lesson covers the first two of those three.

The most common trigger is a record condition, tied directly to a table. You can fire on a record being inserted, a record being updated, or — most often — on one specific field changing to one specific value. The classic example is an Incident notification configured to fire only when the State field changes to Resolved, so the caller hears about exactly the transition that matters to them, not every minor edit along the way.

The second trigger type is event-driven. Somewhere else in the instance, a Business Rule, a Workflow, or a Flow Designer action can call gs.eventQueue to fire a named event into the sysevent table, and a notification can listen for that event name instead of a table condition. This handles situations too complex for a simple field check — an SLA breach based on a time calculation is the standard example. Deep event scripting itself is covered later, in Course 6.

Who will receive it is configured completely separately from the trigger. A notification can send to a field on the record itself, like Caller or Assigned to, to every active member of a specific group, to one fixed user regardless of which record fired it, or to an Email field stored directly on the record. Picking the wrong field here — say, Assigned to when the real audience is the caller — is the single most common reason a correctly-triggered notification still reaches the wrong person.

Beyond the basic trigger, additional filter conditions narrow things further, using the same condition builder as any list filter. State changes to Resolved, and Priority is 1-Critical, and Category is Hardware turns one broad notification into a precisely scoped one. Several narrow, clearly-reasoned notifications almost always beat one broad notification stacked with conditions nobody can fully explain six months later.

Trigger, recipients, and conditions — three independent settings living on the same sysevent_email_action record, and getting any one of them wrong is enough to break the whole notification even when the other two are perfect. Next up: Email Templates, the reusable message body a notification actually references instead of writing its own.
